name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q01 - Opposing external potential in Daniell cell

questiontext.text: In a standard Daniell cell operating at \(298\text{ K}\) with \([\text{Zn}^{2+}] = [\text{Cu}^{2+}] = 1\text{ mol dm}^{-3}\), an external opposing potential \(E_{\text{ext}}\) is applied across the cell. When the opposing potential reaches exactly \(1.1\text{ V}\), what is observed regarding the current and chemical reaction in the cell?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A standard Daniell cell has an electromotive force of \(1.1\text{ V}\). When an external opposing potential \(E_{\text{ext}}\) is applied against the cell potential, it counteracts the driving force of the spontaneous redox reaction.

Step 2: Evaluation of Conditions
When the applied opposing external voltage is less than the cell potential (\(E_{\text{ext}} < 1.1\text{ V}\)), the spontaneous reaction continues, electrons flow from zinc to copper, and current flows from copper to zinc. When the external potential equals the cell potential (\(E_{\text{ext}} = 1.1\text{ V}\)), the net driving potential is zero.

Step 3: Conclusion
At \(E_{\text{ext}} = 1.1\text{ V}\), no net electron transfer takes place across the external circuit, the current drops to zero, and the overall chemical reaction stops completely.

Final Conceptual Answer: No current flows through the circuit and the cell reaction stops altogether.

answer.text: No current flows and no chemical reaction takes place
Electrons flow from copper to zinc and zinc is deposited at the anode
Current flows from copper to zinc at an increased rate
Zinc continues to dissolve and copper continues to deposit normally

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q02 - Behavior of Daniell cell when external potential exceeds cell potential

questiontext.text: When an external opposing voltage \(E_{\text{ext}} > 1.1\text{ V}\) is applied to a standard Daniell cell consisting of zinc and copper electrodes dipped in \(1\text{ M}\) solutions of their respective salts, the cell behaves as:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A galvanic cell generates electrical energy from a spontaneous redox reaction. When an external opposing voltage exceeds the standard electromotive force of the galvanic cell (\(E_{\text{ext}} > 1.1\text{ V}\)), electrical energy from the external source forces the non-spontaneous reverse reaction to occur.

Step 2: Analysis of Polarity and Direction of Flow
Under the influence of the external source with \(E_{\text{ext}} > 1.1\text{ V}\), electrons are pushed from the copper electrode to the zinc electrode. Consequently, conventional electric current flows from zinc to copper.

Step 3: Nature of Electrode Processes
At the zinc electrode, reduction takes place (\(\text{Zn}^{2+} + 2\mathrm{e}^- \rightarrow \text{Zn}\)), depositing zinc. At the copper electrode, oxidation takes place (\(\text{Cu} \rightarrow \text{Cu}^{2+} + 2\mathrm{e}^-\)), dissolving copper. The device now operates as an electrolytic cell.

Final Conceptual Answer: An electrolytic cell where electrons flow from copper to zinc, with zinc depositing at the zinc electrode and copper dissolving at the copper electrode.

answer.text: A galvanic cell where electrons flow from zinc to copper and zinc continues to dissolve
An electrolytic cell where electrons flow from copper to zinc, zinc deposits at the zinc electrode, and copper dissolves
An electrolytic cell where electrons flow from zinc to copper and copper dissolves
A galvanic cell operating at zero net potential with no chemical transformation

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q03 - Current flow and electrode reactions in Daniell cell under low opposing voltage

questiontext.text: In a Daniell cell connected to an opposing external circuit with \(E_{\text{ext}} < 1.1\text{ V}\), which of the following statements correctly describes the flow of current and the electrode processes?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In a galvanic cell, the spontaneous redox reaction is \(\text{Zn(s)} + \text{Cu}^{2+}(\text{aq}) \rightarrow \text{Zn}^{2+}(\text{aq)} + \text{Cu(s)}\). Oxidation occurs at the zinc rod (anode) and reduction occurs at the copper rod (cathode).

Step 2: Direction of Current and Electron Flow
When the opposing external potential is less than \(1.1\text{ V}\) (\(E_{\text{ext}} < 1.1\text{ V}\)), the spontaneous cell reaction dominates. Electrons flow through the external circuit from the zinc rod to the copper rod, meaning conventional electric current flows from the copper rod to the zinc rod.

Step 3: Mass Changes at Electrodes
Zinc atoms lose electrons and dissolve into solution as \(\text{Zn}^{2+}\) ions at the anode, while \(\text{Cu}^{2+}\) ions gain electrons and deposit as metallic copper at the cathode.

Final Conceptual Answer: Conventional current flows from copper to zinc, zinc dissolves at the anode, and copper deposits at the cathode.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q04 - Electrode polarity and IUPAC convention in galvanic cells

questiontext.text: According to IUPAC conventions for galvanic cells, which of the following statements correctly identifies the nature of the anode and cathode and their electrostatic potentials with respect to the solution?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Definition of Anode and Cathode
In any electrochemical cell, the electrode at which oxidation occurs is defined as the anode, and the electrode at which reduction occurs is defined as the cathode.

Step 2: Sign Conventions in Galvanic Cells
In a galvanic cell, metal atoms leave electrons on the anode as they oxidize into solution, giving the anode a negative potential relative to the solution. At the cathode, metal ions take up electrons from the electrode to get reduced, giving the cathode a positive potential relative to the solution.

Step 3: Conclusion
The anode is the site of oxidation and has a negative potential, while the cathode is the site of reduction and has a positive potential.

Final Conceptual Answer: The anode is the electrode where oxidation takes place and has a negative potential with respect to the solution, whereas the cathode is where reduction takes place and has a positive potential.

Oxidation occurs at the cathode which has a negative potential, and reduction occurs at the anode which has a positive potential

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q05 - IUPAC representation of copper silver galvanic cell

For the spontaneous cell reaction:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify Half-Reactions
Oxidation half-reaction: \(\text{Cu(s)} \rightarrow \text{Cu}^{2+}(\text{aq}) + 2\mathrm{e}^-\) (Anode process).
Reduction half-reaction: \(\text{Ag}^{+}(\text{aq}) + \mathrm{e}^- \rightarrow \text{Ag(s)}\) (Cathode process).

Step 2: Apply IUPAC Cell Notation Rules
By IUPAC convention, the anode (oxidation half-cell) is written on the left and the cathode (reduction half-cell) is written on the right.
A single vertical line represents a phase boundary between the solid electrode and the electrolyte.
A double vertical line represents the salt bridge connecting the two electrolyte solutions.

Step 3: Construct Cell Representation
The oxidation half-cell is written as \(\text{Cu(s)} \mid \text{Cu}^{2+}(\text{aq})\).
The reduction half-cell is written as \(\text{Ag}^{+}(\text{aq}) \mid \text{Ag(s)}\).
Joining them across the salt bridge gives: \(\text{Cu(s)} \mid \text{Cu}^{2+}(\text{aq}) \parallel \text{Ag}^{+}(\text{aq}) \mid \text{Ag(s)}\).

Final Conceptual Answer: \(\text{Cu(s)} \mid \text{Cu}^{2+}(\text{aq}) \parallel \text{Ag}^{+}(\text{aq}) \mid \text{Ag(s)}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q06 - Calculation of standard electromotive force of copper silver cell

questiontext.text:
Given the standard reduction potentials:

\[E^\circ_{\text{Ag}^{+}/\text{Ag}} = +0.80\text{ V}\]

\[E^\circ_{\text{Cu}^{2+}/\text{Cu}} = +0.34\text{ V}\]

What is the standard electromotive force (\(E^\circ_{\text{cell}}\)) of the cell \(\text{Cu(s)} \mid \text{Cu}^{2+}(\text{aq}) \parallel \text{Ag}^{+}(\text{aq}) \mid \text{Ag(s)}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Standard reduction potential of cathode (right electrode, silver): \(E^\circ_{\text{right}} = E^\circ_{\text{Ag}^{+}/\text{Ag}} = +0.80\text{ V}\).
Standard reduction potential of anode (left electrode, copper): \(E^\circ_{\text{left}} = E^\circ_{\text{Cu}^{2+}/\text{Cu}} = +0.34\text{ V}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Standard electrode potentials are reduction potentials according to IUPAC convention. The standard cell potential is the standard reduction potential of the cathode minus the standard reduction potential of the anode.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae
\[E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = E^\circ_{\text{right}} - E^\circ_{\text{left}} = E^\circ_{\text{cathode}} - E^\circ_{\text{anode}}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = 0.80\text{ V} - 0.34\text{ V} = +0.46\text{ V}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Since the cell reaction is spontaneous, \(E^\circ_{\text{cell}}\) must be positive, which is confirmed as \(+0.46\text{ V}\).

Final Conceptual Answer: \(+0.46\text{ V}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q07 - Standard conditions and potential of the standard hydrogen electrode

questiontext.text: Which of the following conditions and arbitrary potential values correctly define the Standard Hydrogen Electrode (SHE)?

By international agreement and IUPAC convention, the potential of the standard hydrogen electrode is assigned a value of \(0.00\text{ V}\) at all temperatures.

Final Conceptual Answer: Hydrogen gas at \(1\text{ bar}\), \([\text{H}^{+}] = 1\text{ M}\), with an assigned potential of \(0.00\text{ V}\) at all temperatures.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q08 - Role of inert platinum and gold electrodes in redox systems

questiontext.text: In electrochemical cells, inert electrodes such as platinum or gold are frequently employed (for example in \(\text{Pt(s)} \mid \text{H}_2(\text{g}) \mid \text{H}^{+}(\text{aq})\) or \(\text{Pt(s)} \mid \text{Br}_2(\text{aq}) \mid \text{Br}^{-}(\text{aq})\)). An inert electrode is chemically unreactive under the operating conditions of the half-cell reaction.

Metals like platinum and gold do not take part chemically in the oxidation or reduction reactions (they neither dissolve as ions nor do their cations deposit).

Step 3: Physical Role
They provide a solid conducting surface for the adsorption of reactants, catalyze electron transfer between chemical species, and facilitate the conduction of electrons to and from the external circuit.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q09 - Thermodynamic feasibility of ferric ion redox reactions with halides

questiontext.text:
Given the standard reduction potentials at \(298\text{ K}\):

\[E^\circ_{\text{Fe}^{3+}/\text{Fe}^{2+}} = +0.77\text{ V}\]

\[E^\circ_{\text{I}_2/\text{I}^-} = +0.54\text{ V}\]

\[E^\circ_{\text{Br}_2/\text{Br}^-} = +1.09\text{ V}\]

Which of the following reactions is thermodynamically feasible under standard conditions?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
\(E^\circ_{\text{Fe}^{3+}/\text{Fe}^{2+}} = +0.77\text{ V}\)
\(E^\circ_{\text{I}_2/\text{I}^-} = +0.54\text{ V}\)
\(E^\circ_{\text{Br}_2/\text{Br}^-} = +1.09\text{ V}\)

Step 2: Criterion for Feasibility
A redox reaction is thermodynamically feasible under standard conditions if the overall standard cell potential is positive (\(E^\circ_{\text{cell}} > 0\)), where \(E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = E^\circ_{\text{reduction}} - E^\circ_{\text{oxidation}}\).

Step 3: Evaluation of the Reaction between \(\text{Fe}^{3+}\) and \(\text{I}^-\)
For the reaction \(2\text{Fe}^{3+} + 2\text{I}^- \rightarrow 2\text{Fe}^{2+} + \text{I}_2\):
Reduction: \(\text{Fe}^{3+} + \mathrm{e}^- \rightarrow \text{Fe}^{2+}\), \(E^\circ = +0.77\text{ V}\).
Oxidation: \(2\text{I}^- \rightarrow \text{I}_2 + 2\mathrm{e}^-\), \(E^\circ = +0.54\text{ V}\).
\(E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = 0.77\text{ V} - 0.54\text{ V} = +0.23\text{ V} > 0\). This reaction is spontaneous and feasible.

Step 4: Evaluation of the Reaction between \(\text{Fe}^{3+}\) and \(\text{Br}^-\)
For the reaction \(2\text{Fe}^{3+} + 2\text{Br}^- \rightarrow 2\text{Fe}^{2+} + \text{Br}_2\):
\(E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = 0.77\text{ V} - 1.09\text{ V} = -0.32\text{ V} < 0\). This reaction is non-feasible.

Final Conceptual Answer: The reaction between \(\text{Fe}^{3+}(\text{aq})\) and \(\text{I}^-(\text{aq})\) is feasible, whereas the reaction between \(\text{Fe}^{3+}(\text{aq})\) and \(\text{Br}^-(\text{aq})\) is not feasible.

answer.text: Oxidation of \(\text{I}^{-}(\text{aq})\) by \(\text{Fe}^{3+}(\text{aq})\) is feasible, but oxidation of \(\text{Br}^{-}(\text{aq})\) by \(\text{Fe}^{3+}(\text{aq})\) is not feasible

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q10 - Oxidizing and reducing power trends in electrochemical series

questiontext.text: According to the electrochemical series given in the NCERT textbook, lithium has the most negative standard reduction potential (\(E^\circ_{\text{Li}^+/\text{Li}} = -3.05\text{ V}\)) and fluorine has the most positive (\(E^\circ_{\text{F}_2/\text{F}^-} = +2.87\text{ V}\)). This implies that in aqueous solution:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Standard electrode potentials are listed as reduction potentials. A higher positive \(E^\circ\) indicates a greater tendency of the oxidized form to gain electrons (act as an oxidizing agent).

Step 2: Analysis of the Extreme Values
Fluorine has the highest positive potential (\(+2.87\text{ V}\)), indicating that \(\text{F}_2\) gas has the strongest tendency to be reduced to \(\text{F}^-\), making \(\text{F}_2\) the strongest oxidizing agent.

Step 3: Reducing Power of Lithium
Lithium has the most negative potential (\(-3.05\text{ V}\)), which means \(\text{Li}^+\) is the weakest oxidizing agent, and conversely, metallic lithium has the greatest tendency to lose electrons, making lithium metal the most powerful reducing agent in aqueous solution.

Final Conceptual Answer: Lithium metal is the strongest reducing agent and fluorine gas is the strongest oxidizing agent.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q11 - Displacement order of metals from salt solutions based on potentials

questiontext.text:
Given the standard reduction potentials at \(298\text{ K}\):

\[E^\circ_{\text{Mg}^{2+}/\text{Mg}} = -2.36\text{ V}, \quad E^\circ_{\text{Al}^{3+}/\text{Al}} = -1.66\text{ V}, \quad E^\circ_{\text{Zn}^{2+}/\text{Zn}} = -0.76\text{ V}, \quad E^\circ_{\text{Fe}^{2+}/\text{Fe}} = -0.44\text{ V}, \quad E^\circ_{\text{Cu}^{2+}/\text{Cu}} = +0.34\text{ V}\]

Which of the following represents the correct order in which each metal can displace the succeeding metals from their aqueous salt solutions?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Principle
A metal with a more negative standard reduction potential has a greater reducing power and can displace a metal with a less negative (or positive) reduction potential from its aqueous salt solution.

Step 2: Comparison of Standard Reduction Potentials
\(\text{Mg}^{2+}/\text{Mg}\) (\(-2.36\text{ V}\)) < \(\text{Al}^{3+}/\text{Al}\) (\(-1.66\text{ V}\)) < \(\text{Zn}^{2+}/\text{Zn}\) (\(-0.76\text{ V}\)) < \(\text{Fe}^{2+}/\text{Fe}\) (\(-0.44\text{ V}\)) < \(\text{Cu}^{2+}/\text{Cu}\) (\(+0.34\text{ V}\)).

Step 3: Establishing Displacement Order
Magnesium has the strongest reducing tendency and displaces aluminium, zinc, iron, and copper. Aluminium displaces zinc, iron, and copper. Zinc displaces iron and copper. Iron displaces copper. Thus, the order of displacing power is \(\text{Mg} > \text{Al} > \text{Zn} > \text{Fe} > \text{Cu}\).

Final Conceptual Answer: \(\text{Mg} > \text{Al} > \text{Zn} > \text{Fe} > \text{Cu}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q12 - Electrochemical basis of copper dissolution in nitric acid versus hydrochloric acid

questiontext.text: Metallic copper does not dissolve in dilute hydrochloric acid to liberate hydrogen gas, but it readily dissolves in nitric acid. What is the fundamental electrochemical reason for this behavior?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle of Acid Dissolution
For a metal to dissolve in an acid by liberating hydrogen gas, the metal must be oxidized by \(\text{H}^{+}\) ions: \(\text{M} + n\text{H}^{+} \rightarrow \text{M}^{n+} + \frac{n}{2}\text{H}_2\). This requires the standard reduction potential of the metal couple to be lower (more negative) than that of the \(\text{H}^{+}/\text{H}_2\) couple (\(0.00\text{ V}\)).

Step 2: Interaction with Hydrochloric Acid
The standard potential of copper is \(E^\circ_{\text{Cu}^{2+}/\text{Cu}} = +0.34\text{ V}\), which is positive relative to the standard hydrogen electrode. Therefore, \(\text{H}^{+}\) ions cannot oxidize metallic copper under standard conditions, so copper does not dissolve in \(\text{HCl}\).

Step 3: Interaction with Nitric Acid
Nitric acid contains nitrate ions (\(\text{NO}_3^-\)), which have a much higher standard reduction potential (\(E^\circ_{\text{NO}_3^-/\text{NO}} = +0.97\text{ V}\)) than \(\text{Cu}^{2+}/\text{Cu}\) (\(+0.34\text{ V}\)). Copper is oxidized by the nitrate ion rather than by the hydrogen ion.

Final Conceptual Answer: Copper has a positive reduction potential and cannot be oxidized by \(\text{H}^{+}\) ions, but is oxidized by nitrate ions in nitric acid.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q13 - Calculation of cell potential using Nernst equation for magnesium silver cell

questiontext.text:
A galvanic cell operates based on the reaction:

\[\text{Mg(s)} + 2\text{Ag}^{+}(0.0001\text{ M}) \rightarrow \text{Mg}^{2+}(0.130\text{ M}) + 2\text{Ag(s)}\]

Given that \(E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = 3.17\text{ V}\) and \(\frac{2.303RT}{F} = 0.059\text{ V}\) at \(298\text{ K}\), what is the electromotive force (\(E_{\text{cell}}\)) of the cell?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Standard cell potential: \(E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = 3.17\text{ V}\).
Electrode reaction: \(\text{Mg(s)} + 2\text{Ag}^{+}(\text{aq}) \rightarrow \text{Mg}^{2+}(\text{aq}) + 2\text{Ag(s)}\).
Number of electrons transferred: \(n = 2\).
Concentrations: \([\text{Mg}^{2+}] = 0.130\text{ M}\), \([\text{Ag}^{+}] = 0.0001\text{ M} = 10^{-4}\text{ M}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Model
Apply the Nernst equation at \(T = 298\text{ K}\) where solid magnesium and silver have activities equal to unity.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae
\[E_{\text{cell}} = E^\circ_{\text{cell}} - \frac{0.059}{n} \log \frac{[\text{Mg}^{2+}]}{[\text{Ag}^{+}]^2}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate the reaction quotient term:
\[Q = \frac{[\text{Mg}^{2+}]}{[\text{Ag}^{+}]^2} = \frac{0.130}{(10^{-4})^2} = \frac{0.130}{10^{-8}} = 1.30 \times 10^7\]
Evaluate the logarithm:
\[\log(1.30 \times 10^7) = \log(1.30) + 7 \approx 0.1139 + 7 = 7.114\]
Calculate the subtraction term:
\[\frac{0.059}{2} \times 7.114 \approx 0.0295 \times 7.114 \approx 0.21\text{ V}\]
Substitute into the Nernst equation:
\[E_{\text{cell}} = 3.17\text{ V} - 0.21\text{ V} = 2.96\text{ V}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The potential decreases from \(3.17\text{ V}\) to \(2.96\text{ V}\) because the reaction quotient \(Q > 1\), as expected from Le Chatelier's principle and Nernst equation.

Final Conceptual Answer: \(2.96\text{ V}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q14 - Effect of ion concentrations on Daniell cell potential

questiontext.text:
For the Daniell cell operating at \(298\text{ K}\) according to the reaction:

\[\text{Zn(s)} + \text{Cu}^{2+}(\text{aq}) \rightarrow \text{Zn}^{2+}(\text{aq)} + \text{Cu(s)}\]

How does the cell electromotive force (\(E_{\text{cell}}\)) vary when the concentration of \(\text{Cu}^{2+}\) ions is increased while the concentration of \(\text{Zn}^{2+}\) ions is decreased?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Relevant Principle and Formula
The Nernst equation for the Daniell cell at \(298\text{ K}\) is given by: \[E_{\text{cell}} = E^\circ_{\text{cell}} - \frac{0.059}{2} \log \frac{[\text{Zn}^{2+}]}{[\text{Cu}^{2+}]}\]

Step 2: Analysis of the Concentration Ratio
The logarithmic term depends directly on the ratio of product ion concentration to reactant ion concentration: \(Q = \frac{[\text{Zn}^{2+}]}{[\text{Cu}^{2+}]}\).
When \([\text{Cu}^{2+}]\) increases and \([\text{Zn}^{2+}]\) decreases, the reaction quotient \(Q\) decreases significantly.

Step 3: Effect on Cell Potential
As \(Q\) decreases, \(\log Q\) becomes smaller (or more negative), which reduces the value being subtracted from \(E^\circ_{\text{cell}}\) (or adds to it). Consequently, the value of \(E_{\text{cell}}\) increases.

Final Conceptual Answer: The cell potential increases when the copper ion concentration increases and the zinc ion concentration decreases.

answer.text: The cell potential \(E_{\text{cell}}\) decreases
The cell potential \(E_{\text{cell}}\) increases
The cell potential remains strictly constant at \(1.10\text{ V}\)
The cell potential drops to zero immediately

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q15 - Electrode potential calculation of hydrogen electrode at specified pH

questiontext.text: What is the electrode potential of a hydrogen electrode at \(298\text{ K}\) dipping in an aqueous solution of \(\text{pH} = 10\) under a hydrogen gas pressure of \(1\text{ bar}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
\(\text{pH} = 10\).
Hydrogen gas pressure: \(p_{\text{H}_2} = 1\text{ bar}\).
Temperature: \(T = 298\text{ K}\).
Electrode reaction (reduction): \(\text{H}^{+}(\text{aq}) + \mathrm{e}^- \rightarrow \frac{1}{2}\text{H}_2(\text{g})\).
Standard reduction potential: \(E^\circ_{\text{H}^{+}/\text{H}_2} = 0.00\text{ V}\).
Number of electrons: \(n = 1\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Model
Activity of pure gas at \(1\text{ bar}\) is unity. From the definition of pH, \([\text{H}^{+}] = 10^{-\text{pH}} = 10^{-10}\text{ M}\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae
By Nernst equation for the hydrogen electrode reduction: \[E_{\text{H}^{+}/\text{H}_2} = E^\circ_{\text{H}^{+}/\text{H}_2} - \frac{0.059}{1} \log \frac{1}{[\text{H}^{+}]}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q16 - General Nernst equation formulation for multi electron cell reactions

For a general electrochemical reaction occurring in a galvanic cell:

\[a\text{A} + b\text{B} \xrightarrow{n\mathrm{e}^-} c\text{C} + d\text{D}\]

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q24 - Intensive and extensive nature of cell potential and Gibbs energy

Electrode potential and cell potential (\(E_{\text{cell}}\)) are intensive properties, meaning their values do not depend on the size of the system or the stoichiometric coefficients chosen to write the reaction equation.
Gibbs free energy change (\(\Delta_r G\)) is an extensive thermodynamic property, meaning its value depends directly on the amount of substance reacting (proportional to stoichiometric coefficients and the number of moles of electrons transferred, \(n\)).

Final Conceptual Answer: \(E^\circ_{\text{cell}}\) is identical for both reactions because it is an intensive property, but \(\Delta_r G^\circ\) doubles for Reaction 2 because it is an extensive property.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q25 - Temperature dependence of metallic versus electrolytic electrical conductance

questiontext.text: How does electrical conductance change with an increase in temperature for metallic (electronic) conductors and electrolytic (ionic) solutions, respectively?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Mechanism of Metallic Conductance
In metallic conductors, current is carried by mobile free electrons moving through a lattice of positive metal ions (kernels). As temperature rises, thermal vibrations of the metal kernels increase, which impedes the flow of electrons through increased scattering. Hence, metallic conductance decreases with increasing temperature.

Step 2: Mechanism of Electrolytic Conductance
In electrolytic solutions, current is carried by ions moving through a solvent. As temperature increases: (i) the viscosity of the solvent decreases, reducing drag on moving ions; (ii) the kinetic energy and mobility of ions increase; (iii) the degree of dissociation of weak electrolytes increases. Hence, electrolytic conductance increases with increasing temperature.

Step 3: Conclusion
Metallic conductance decreases with increasing temperature, whereas electrolytic conductance increases with increasing temperature.

Final Conceptual Answer: Metallic conductance decreases while electrolytic conductance increases with increase in temperature.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q26 - SI unit and conversion relation for electrolytic conductivity

questiontext.text: What is the SI unit of electrolytic conductivity (\(\kappa\)), and how is it related to its commonly used submultiple unit \(\text{S cm}^{-1}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Definition of Conductivity
Conductivity (\(\kappa\)) is the reciprocal of electrical resistivity (\(\rho\)): \[\kappa = \frac{1}{\rho}\] Since resistivity has the SI unit \(\Omega\text{ m}\), conductivity has the SI unit \(\Omega^{-1}\text{ m}^{-1}\).

Step 2: SI Unit of Conductance
In the SI system, \(\Omega^{-1}\) is named siemens (\(\text{S}\)). Thus, the SI unit of conductivity is \(\text{S m}^{-1}\).

Step 3: Conversion to Submultiple Unit
\[1\text{ S cm}^{-1} = \frac{1\text{ S}}{10^{-2}\text{ m}} = 100\text{ S m}^{-1}\] Equivalently, \(1\text{ S m}^{-1} = 0.01\text{ S cm}^{-1}\).

Final Conceptual Answer: The SI unit is \(\text{S m}^{-1}\), and \(1\text{ S cm}^{-1} = 100\text{ S m}^{-1}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q29 - Determination and significance of conductivity cell constant

In practical conductivity cells, measuring the exact distance \(l\) between platinized electrodes and their effective surface area \(A\) is not only inconvenient but also unreliable due to electrode roughness, coating porosity, and irregular cell geometry.

The cell constant is reliably determined by measuring the resistance \(R\) of the cell when filled with a standard solution of potassium chloride (\(\text{KCl}\)) whose conductivity \(\kappa\) has been precisely determined at that temperature: \[G^* = R \times \kappa\]

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q34 - Fundamental reason for conductivity decrease upon electrolytic dilution

questiontext.text: Why does the conductivity (\(\kappa\)) of an electrolytic solution always decrease upon dilution for both strong and weak electrolytes?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Definition of Conductivity
Conductivity (\(\kappa\)) is defined as the conductance of unit volume (\(1\text{ m}^3\) or \(1\text{ cm}^3\)) of an electrolytic solution placed between electrodes of unit cross-sectional area separated by unit distance.

Step 2: Effect of Dilution
When a solution is diluted by adding more solvent, the total volume increases while the number of moles of electrolyte remains fixed (or dissociates only partially more in weak electrolytes).

Step 3: Number of Current Carriers per Unit Volume
As a result of the volume increase, the number of current-carrying ions present per unit volume of solution decreases. Since conductivity depends directly on the concentration of charge carriers per unit volume, conductivity always decreases with dilution.

Final Conceptual Answer: The number of ions per unit volume that carry electric current decreases upon dilution.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q35 - Opposing effects governing molar conductivity increase during dilution

questiontext.text: While conductivity (\(\kappa\)) decreases on dilution, molar conductivity (\(\Lambda_m\)) increases with decrease in concentration. Which of the following statements correctly explains this phenomenon?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Molar conductivity is related to conductivity and volume by: \[\Lambda_m = \kappa V\] where \(V\) is the volume of solution containing one mole of electrolyte.

Step 2: Interplay Between Conductivity and Volume
On dilution, the conductivity \(\kappa\) decreases because the number of ions per unit volume decreases. However, the volume \(V\) containing one mole of electrolyte increases simultaneously.

Step 3: Dominance of Volume Expansion
Experimental observations establish that the increase in volume \(V\) on dilution more than compensates for the decrease in \(\kappa\). Additionally, for weak electrolytes, dilution increases the degree of dissociation (\(\alpha\)), further increasing the total number of ions produced per mole of electrolyte.

Final Conceptual Answer: The decrease in conductivity on dilution is more than compensated by the increase in the volume containing one mole of electrolyte.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q36 - Physical determinants of Debye Huckel Onsager slope constant

questiontext.text:
For strong electrolytes, the variation of molar conductivity with concentration is described by the equation:

\[\Lambda_m = \Lambda_m^\circ - A c^{1/2}\]

What determines the value of the constant \(A\) for a given solvent and temperature?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The Debye-Hückel-Onsager equation models the concentration dependence of molar conductivity for strong electrolytes: \[\Lambda_m = \Lambda_m^\circ - A c^{1/2}\]

Step 2: Physical Basis of Constant \(A\)
The slope constant \(A\) arises from interionic attractions (electrophoretic and relaxation effects) that retard the movement of ions as concentration increases.

Step 3: Dependence on Electrolyte Type
For a specified solvent and temperature, the value of \(A\) depends strictly on the charges of the cation and anion produced upon dissociation (i.e., the valence type of the electrolyte). All electrolytes of a given stoichiometric charge type—such as 1-1 electrolytes (\(\text{NaCl}, \text{KCl}\)), 2-1 electrolytes (\(\text{CaCl}_2\)), or 2-2 electrolytes (\(\text{MgSO}_4\))—have the same value of \(A\).

Final Conceptual Answer: The type of electrolyte, specifically the charges on the cation and anion produced on dissociation.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q37 - Graphical interpretation of intercept and slope in Onsager plots

The graph below illustrates the variation of molar conductivity (\(\Lambda_m\)) with \(c^{1/2}\) for aqueous solutions of \(\text{KCl}\) and \(\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}\):

From such a linear plot, the y-intercept at \(c^{1/2} = 0\) and the negative of the slope represent:

Step 1: Mathematical Model
The Debye-Hückel-Onsager relation for a strong electrolyte is: \[\Lambda_m = \Lambda_m^\circ - A c^{1/2}\] Comparing this to the standard linear equation \(y = mx + c\): \(y = \Lambda_m\), \(x = c^{1/2}\), slope \(m = -A\), and y-intercept \(= \Lambda_m^\circ\).

Step 2: Interpretation of the Intercept
At \(c^{1/2} = 0\) (which corresponds to concentration approaching zero, or infinite dilution), the y-intercept represents the limiting molar conductivity \(\Lambda_m^\circ\) (for \(\text{KCl}\), \(\Lambda_m^\circ = 150.0\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\)).

The slope of the line is negative (\(-A\)). Therefore, the negative of the slope gives the Onsager constant \(A\) (for \(\text{KCl}\), \(A = 87.46\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1} / (\text{mol L}^{-1})^{1/2}\)).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q38 - Limiting molar conductivity calculation for calcium chloride and magnesium sulphate

questiontext.text:
Given the limiting molar conductivities of individual ions at \(298\text{ K}\):

\[\lambda^\circ(\text{Ca}^{2+}) = 119.0\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}, \quad \lambda^\circ(\text{Cl}^-) = 76.3\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\]

\[\lambda^\circ(\text{Mg}^{2+}) = 106.0\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}, \quad \lambda^\circ(\text{SO}_4^{2-}) = 160.0\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\]

What are the limiting molar conductivities (\(\Lambda_m^\circ\)) of \(\text{CaCl}_2\) and \(\text{MgSO}_4\), respectively?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Kohlrausch's law of independent migration of ions states that the limiting molar conductivity of an electrolyte is the sum of the individual contributions of its constituent cations and anions: \[\Lambda_m^\circ = \nu_+ \lambda_+^\circ + \nu_- \lambda_-^\circ\]

Step 2: Calculation for Calcium Chloride
\(\text{CaCl}_2\) dissociates into one \(\text{Ca}^{2+}\) and two \(\text{Cl}^-\) ions (\(\nu_+ = 1, \nu_- = 2\)): \[\Lambda_m^\circ(\text{CaCl}_2) = \lambda^\circ(\text{Ca}^{2+}) + 2\lambda^\circ(\text{Cl}^-)\] \[\Lambda_m^\circ(\text{CaCl}_2) = 119.0 + 2(76.3) = 119.0 + 152.6 = 271.6\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\]

Step 3: Calculation for Magnesium Sulphate
\(\text{MgSO}_4\) dissociates into one \(\text{Mg}^{2+}\) and one \(\text{SO}_4^{2-}\) ion (\(\nu_+ = 1, \nu_- = 1\)): \[\Lambda_m^\circ(\text{MgSO}_4) = \lambda^\circ(\text{Mg}^{2+}) + \lambda^\circ(\text{SO}_4^{2-})\] \[\Lambda_m^\circ(\text{MgSO}_4) = 106.0 + 160.0 = 266.0\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\]

Final Conceptual Answer: \(271.6\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\) for \(\text{CaCl}_2\) and \(266.0\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\) for \(\text{MgSO}_4\).

questiontext.text: Why can the limiting molar conductivity (\(\Lambda_m^\circ\)) of a weak electrolyte like acetic acid NOT be determined experimentally by extrapolating the plot of \(\Lambda_m\) versus \(c^{1/2}\) to zero concentration?

Weak electrolytes have low degree of dissociation (\(\alpha \ll 1\)) at moderate concentrations. As dilution increases, Ostwald's dilution law dictates that \(\alpha\) increases, dramatically increasing the number of ions per mole of electrolyte.

At extremely high dilution where dissociation is complete, the concentration of ions is so low that the conductivity of the solution becomes too small to be measured accurately.

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate molar conductivity: \[\Lambda_m = \frac{4.95 \times 10^{-5}\text{ S cm}^{-1} \times 1000\text{ cm}^3\text{ L}^{-1}}{0.001028\text{ mol L}^{-1}} = \frac{0.0495}{0.001028} \approx 48.15\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\] Calculate degree of dissociation: \[\alpha = \frac{48.15}{390.5} \approx 0.1233\] Calculate dissociation constant: \[K_a = \frac{0.001028 \times (0.1233)^2}{1 - 0.1233} = \frac{0.001028 \times 0.015203}{0.8767} \approx 1.78 \times 10^{-5}\text{ mol L}^{-1}\]

(Molar masses: \(\text{Ag} = 108\text{ g mol}^{-1}\), \(\text{Cu} = 63.5\text{ g mol}^{-1}\), \(\text{Zn} = 65.4\text{ g mol}^{-1}\), \(F = 96500\text{ C mol}^{-1}\))

Mass of silver: \(m_{\text{Ag}} = 1.45\text{ g}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q47 - Comparison of electrolysis products for molten versus aqueous sodium chloride

questiontext.text: What are the primary products formed at the cathode and anode during the electrolysis of molten \(\text{NaCl}\) and aqueous \(\text{NaCl}\) solution (using inert electrodes), respectively?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Electrolysis of Molten \(\text{NaCl}\)
In molten \(\text{NaCl}\), only \(\text{Na}^{+}\) cations and \(\text{Cl}^{-}\) anions are present. Cathode: \(\text{Na}^{+} + \mathrm{e}^- \rightarrow \text{Na(s)}\) (metallic sodium is formed). Anode: \(\text{Cl}^- \rightarrow \frac{1}{2}\text{Cl}_2(\text{g}) + \mathrm{e}^-\) (chlorine gas is evolved).

Step 2: Electrolysis of Aqueous \(\text{NaCl}\)
In aqueous solution, water molecules and their dissociation products compete with sodium and chloride ions. At cathode: Reduction of \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\) to form \(\text{H}_2(\text{g})\) (\(E^\circ = 0.00\text{ V}\) for \(\text{H}^+\)) occurs preferentially over \(\text{Na}^+\) (\(E^\circ = -2.71\text{ V}\)). At anode: Chloride oxidation to \(\text{Cl}_2(\text{g})\) occurs preferentially due to the overpotential of oxygen. The residual solution contains \(\text{NaOH}\).

Step 3: Conclusion
Molten \(\text{NaCl}\) yields \(\text{Na}\) at cathode and \(\text{Cl}_2\) at anode; aqueous \(\text{NaCl}\) yields \(\text{H}_2\) at cathode, \(\text{Cl}_2\) at anode, and \(\text{NaOH}\) in solution.

Final Conceptual Answer: Molten \(\text{NaCl}\) produces sodium and chlorine; aqueous \(\text{NaCl}\) produces hydrogen, chlorine, and sodium hydroxide.

Molten yields hydrogen and oxygen; aqueous yields sodium metal and chlorine gas
Molten yields sodium and chlorine; aqueous yields hydrogen, chlorine, and aqueous sodium hydroxide

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q48 - Kinetic overpotential rationale for chlorine discharge in aqueous electrolysis

questiontext.text:
During the electrolysis of aqueous \(\text{NaCl}\), the standard oxidation potentials are:

\[2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightarrow \text{O}_2(\text{g}) + 4\text{H}^{+}(\text{aq}) + 4\mathrm{e}^-, \quad E^\circ = +1.23\text{ V}\]

\[\text{Cl}^{-}(\text{aq}) \rightarrow \frac{1}{2}\text{Cl}_2(\text{g}) + \mathrm{e}^-, \quad E^\circ = +1.36\text{ V}\]

Thermodynamically, water oxidation has a lower standard potential and should occur preferentially. Why is chlorine gas evolved at the anode instead of oxygen gas?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principles
Standard electrode potential comparison suggests that oxidation of water to \(\text{O}_2\) (\(E^\circ = 1.23\text{ V}\)) should occur at a lower voltage than oxidation of chloride to \(\text{Cl}_2\) (\(E^\circ = 1.36\text{ V}\)).

Step 2: Kinetic Limitations and Overpotential
Although water oxidation is thermodynamically favored, the oxidation of water to produce oxygen gas involves a complex multi-step four-electron transfer process that is kinetically very slow.

Step 3: Role of Overpotential
Because of the slow kinetics, oxygen evolution requires an extra potential known as overpotential (overvoltage) to proceed at an appreciable rate. This overpotential raises the practical discharge voltage of water well above \(1.36\text{ V}\), making the oxidation of chloride ions to \(\text{Cl}_2\) gas kinetically and practically preferred.

Final Conceptual Answer: Oxidation of water to oxygen is kinetically slow and requires a significant overpotential, making chloride oxidation preferred.

Oxygen gas dissolves completely into the sodium hydroxide solution without bubbling out
Water oxidation is endothermic while chloride oxidation is highly exothermic
Oxidation of water is kinetically slow and requires a significant overpotential

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q49 - Anodic oxidation products during electrolysis of dilute versus concentrated sulphuric acid

questiontext.text: During the electrolysis of aqueous sulphuric acid using platinum electrodes, which of the following correctly describes the oxidation product formed at the anode for dilute \(\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\) and concentrated \(\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\), respectively?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Possible Anodic Reactions
Two oxidation processes can occur at the anode: (i) Oxidation of water: \[2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightarrow \text{O}_2(\text{g}) + 4\text{H}^{+}(\text{aq}) + 4\mathrm{e}^-, \quad E^\circ = +1.23\text{ V}\] (ii) Oxidation of sulphate ion: \[2\text{SO}_4^{2-}(\text{aq}) \rightarrow \text{S}_2\text{O}_8^{2-}(\text{aq}) + 2\mathrm{e}^-, \quad E^\circ = +1.96\text{ V}\]

Step 2: Dilute Sulphuric Acid Behavior
In dilute sulphuric acid, water molecules are present in overwhelming concentration and the lower electrode potential (\(+1.23\text{ V}\)) favors the oxidation of water, evolving oxygen gas (\(\text{O}_2\)).

Step 3: Concentrated Sulphuric Acid Behavior
In concentrated sulphuric acid, the concentration of \(\text{SO}_4^{2-}\) (or \(\text{HSO}_4^-\)) is very high. Under these conditions, oxidation of sulphate to peroxodisulphate ion (\(\text{S}_2\text{O}_8^{2-}\)) becomes predominant at the anode.

Final Conceptual Answer: Dilute sulphuric acid yields oxygen gas, whereas concentrated sulphuric acid yields peroxodisulphate ions.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q50 - Electrochemical basis of voltage constancy in miniature mercury cells

questiontext.text: The cell potential of a miniature mercury cell remains practically constant at approximately \(1.35\text{ V}\) throughout its entire operating life. What is the fundamental chemical reason for this constant potential?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Overall Cell Reaction
The overall chemical reaction occurring in a mercury cell during discharge is: \[\text{Zn(Hg)} + \text{HgO(s)} \rightarrow \text{ZnO(s)} + \text{Hg(l)}\]

Step 2: Analysis of Participating Species
Zinc is present as an amalgam, mercury(II) oxide is a solid, zinc oxide is an insoluble solid, and mercury is a pure liquid.

Step 3: Influence on Nernst Equation
The overall reaction does not involve any dissolved ionic species in solution whose concentration can vary or change during the cell's lifetime. Because all reactants and products remain in standard states of unit activity, the cell potential does not change as the cell discharges.

Final Conceptual Answer: The overall cell reaction does not involve any dissolved ion whose concentration can change during its life.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q51 - Electrode transformations during recharging of secondary lead storage batteries

questiontext.text: Which of the following correctly describes the chemical changes occurring at the electrodes when a secondary lead storage battery is being recharged by passing current in the reverse direction?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Reactions During Discharge
During discharge, lead at the anode is oxidized to \(\text{PbSO}_4(\text{s})\): \[\text{Pb(s)} + \text{SO}_4^{2-}(\text{aq}) \rightarrow \text{PbSO}_4(\text{s)} + 2\mathrm{e}^-\] At the cathode, \(\text{PbO}_2(\text{s})\) is reduced to \(\text{PbSO}_4(\text{s})\): \[\text{PbO}_2(\text{s)} + \text{SO}_4^{2-}(\text{aq}) + 4\text{H}^{+}(\text{aq}) + 2\mathrm{e}^- \rightarrow \text{PbSO}_4(\text{s)} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\]

Step 2: Recharging Process
Recharging reverses the flow of electrons, forcing the non-spontaneous reverse reactions to take place. At the negative plate (now cathode): \(\text{PbSO}_4(\text{s})\) is reduced back to metallic spongy lead (\(\text{Pb}\)). At the positive plate (now anode): \(\text{PbSO}_4(\text{s})\) is oxidized back to lead dioxide (\(\text{PbO}_2\)).

Step 3: Regeneration of Electrolyte
Sulphuric acid is regenerated during recharging, increasing the density of the electrolytic solution.

Final Conceptual Answer: \(\text{PbSO}_4\) on the anode is converted to \(\text{Pb}\), and \(\text{PbSO}_4\) on the cathode is converted to \(\text{PbO}_2\), with regeneration of \(\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q52 - Electrochemical mechanism and standard cell potential of atmospheric iron corrosion

questiontext.text:
The rusting of iron in the atmosphere is an electrochemical process. At a specific anodic spot, iron is oxidised according to:

\[2\text{Fe(s)} \rightarrow 2\text{Fe}^{2+} + 4\mathrm{e}^-, \quad E^\circ = -0.44\text{ V}\]

Which reaction represents the process taking place at the cathodic spot, and what is the overall standard cell potential for the corrosion cell?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principles
Corrosion of iron involves localized electrochemical cells set up on the metallic surface in the presence of moisture and atmospheric oxygen.

Step 2: Anodic Spot
At an anodic spot (often an impurity, strain, or scratch), iron is oxidised: \[2\text{Fe(s)} \rightarrow 2\text{Fe}^{2+} + 4\mathrm{e}^-, \quad E^\circ_{\text{Fe}^{2+}/\text{Fe}} = -0.44\text{ V}\]

Step 3: Cathodic Spot
Electrons released at the anodic spot travel through the conducting iron metal to another spot. In the presence of \(\text{H}^{+}\) ions (derived from carbonic acid formed by dissolved atmospheric \(\text{CO}_2\)), dissolved oxygen is reduced: \[\text{O}_2(\text{g}) + 4\text{H}^{+}(\text{aq}) + 4\mathrm{e}^- \rightarrow 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l), \quad E^\circ = +1.23\text{ V}\]

Step 4: Overall Cell Reaction and Standard Potential
Adding the anodic and cathodic half-reactions: \[2\text{Fe(s)} + \text{O}_2(\text{g}) + 4\text{H}^{+}(\text{aq}) \rightarrow 2\text{Fe}^{2+}(\text{aq)} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\] The standard cell potential is: \[E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = E^\circ_{\text{cathode}} - E^\circ_{\text{anode}} = 1.23\text{ V} - (-0.44\text{ V}) = +1.67\text{ V}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The cathodic reaction is \(\text{O}_2(\text{g}) + 4\text{H}^{+}(\text{aq}) + 4\mathrm{e}^- \rightarrow 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\) and \(E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = 1.67\text{ V}\).

Final Conceptual Answer: \(\text{O}_2(\text{g}) + 4\text{H}^{+}(\text{aq}) + 4\mathrm{e}^- \rightarrow 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\) with \(E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = 1.67\text{ V}\).
